summary.text: Factoring into coprime prime powers shows that if $2^k\mid\varphi(m)$, then either $m\ge 2^{k+1}$ or $m$ is a product of distinct Fermat primes whose indices $j$ satisfy $k\le\sum 2^j$; the latter alternative arises because a prime of the exceptional form $2^k+1$ must be a Fermat prime. Taking $k=2^n$ and applying the geometric-sum bound forces either the sole factor $F_n$ or the same lower bound $2^{2^n+1}$, while the totient formulas for $F_n$ and for a power of two provide the corresponding upper bounds.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(r)=\min\{m\in\mathbb N:m>0\text{ and }2^r\mid\varphi(m)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. Also write
\[
F_j=2^{2^j}+1
\]
for the \(j\)-th Fermat number. We prove the stronger assertion that, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
A(2^n)=
\begin{cases}
F_n,&\text{if }F_n\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^n+1},&\text{if }F_n\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]
Taking \(n=33\) gives exactly the desired statement.

The main point is a lower bound for every integer whose totient is divisible by a specified power of two.

## 1. A structural lemma

We first prove the following claim.

**Structural lemma.** Let \(m>0\), and suppose that \(2^k\mid\varphi(m)\). Then at least one of the following holds:

1. \(m\ge 2^{k+1}\);
2. there is a finite set \(S\) of nonnegative integers such that every \(F_j\), \(j\in S\), is prime,
   \[
   m=\prod_{j\in S}F_j,
   \tag{2}
   \]
   and
   \[
   k\le \sum_{j\in S}2^j.
   \tag{3}
   \]

Thus, the only possible exceptions to the elementary lower bound \(m\ge 2^{k+1}\) are squarefree products of distinct Fermat primes.

We prove this first for prime powers and then show that it is preserved under multiplication of coprime integers.

### Prime powers

Let \(m=p^r\), where \(p\) is prime and \(r\ge1\). Recall that
\[
\varphi(p^r)=p^{r-1}(p-1).
\tag{4}
\]

If \(p=2\), then \(\varphi(2^r)=2^{r-1}\). Hence \(2^k\mid\varphi(2^r)\) implies \(k\le r-1\), and therefore
\[
2^{k+1}\le 2^r=m.
\]
So the first alternative holds.

Now suppose that \(p\) is odd. Since \(p^{r-1}\) is odd, (4) and \(2^k\mid\varphi(p^r)\) imply
\[
2^k\mid p-1.
\]
Write
\[
p-1=2^k t,
\tag{5}
\]
where \(t\ge1\). In particular, \(p\ge 2^k+1\).

If \(r\ge2\), then
\[
m=p^r\ge p^2\ge(2^k+1)^2\ge 2^{k+1}.
\]
Indeed, \((2^k+1)^2\ge 2\cdot2^k=2^{k+1}\). Thus again the first alternative holds.

It remains to consider \(r=1\), so \(m=p\). If \(t\ge2\), then by (5)
\[
p=2^k t+1>2^{k+1},
\]
and the first alternative holds.

The only remaining case is \(r=1\) and \(t=1\). Then
\[
p=2^k+1.
\tag{6}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(k\ne0\). A standard elementary factorization now shows that if \(2^k+1\) is prime, then \(k\) must be a power of two. For completeness, write
\[
k=2^j u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u>1\), then, with \(x=2^{2^j}>1\),
\[
2^k+1=x^u+1=(x+1)(x^{u-1}-x^{u-2}+\cdots-x+1),
\]
which is a nontrivial factorization. Thus primality forces \(u=1\), so \(k=2^j\) for some \(j\). Equation (6) becomes
\[
p=2^{2^j}+1=F_j.
\]
Taking \(S=\{j\}\), we obtain (2), every Fermat number indexed by \(S\) is prime, and
\[
k=2^j=\sum_{i\in S}2^i.
\]
This is precisely the second alternative.

Consequently, the structural lemma holds for every prime power.

### Coprime products

Suppose now that the structural lemma holds for integers \(a>1\) and \(b>1\), and assume \(\gcd(a,b)=1\). We show that it holds for \(m=ab\).

Write the exact powers of two in the two totients as
\[
\varphi(a)=2^{k_a}u,
\qquad
\varphi(b)=2^{k_b}v,
\]
where \(u\) and \(v\) are odd. Since \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime, Euler's totient is multiplicative, so
\[
\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)=2^{k_a+k_b}uv.
\]
Because \(uv\) is odd, the assumption \(2^k\mid\varphi(ab)\) implies
\[
k\le k_a+k_b.
\tag{7}
\]

We will also use the elementary estimate
\[
2^{k_a}\le a,
\qquad
2^{k_b}\le b.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, \(2^{k_a}\mid\varphi(a)\) and \(\varphi(a)>0\), so \(2^{k_a}\le\varphi(a)\le a\); the proof for \(b\) is the same.

Apply the structural lemma to \(a\), using \(2^{k_a}\mid\varphi(a)\). If its first alternative holds, then \(a\ge2^{k_a+1}\). By (7) and (8),
\[
ab\ge 2^{k_a+1}2^{k_b}=2^{k_a+k_b+1}\ge2^{k+1}.
\]
Thus the first alternative holds for \(ab\). The same argument applies if the first alternative holds for \(b\).

We are left with the case in which both \(a\) and \(b\) have the exceptional form. Thus there are finite sets \(S_a,S_b\) such that
\[
a=\prod_{j\in S_a}F_j,
\qquad
b=\prod_{j\in S_b}F_j,
\]
every Fermat number appearing in either product is prime, and
\[
k_a\le\sum_{j\in S_a}2^j,
\qquad
k_b\le\sum_{j\in S_b}2^j.
\tag{9}
\]
The sets \(S_a\) and \(S_b\) must be disjoint. Otherwise some \(F_j>1\) would divide both \(a\) and \(b\), contradicting \(\gcd(a,b)=1\). Hence
\[
ab=\prod_{j\in S_a\cup S_b}F_j.
\]
Moreover, by (7), (9), and disjointness,
\[
k\le k_a+k_b
 \le \sum_{j\in S_a}2^j+\sum_{j\in S_b}2^j
 =\sum_{j\in S_a\cup S_b}2^j.
\]
Thus the second alternative holds for \(ab\).

Finally, every positive integer is either \(1\), a prime power, or a product of two smaller coprime integers obtained by grouping its distinct prime-power factors. Starting from the prime-power result and repeatedly applying the coprime-product argument proves the structural lemma for every \(m>0\). The case \(m=1\) is harmless: \(\varphi(1)=1\), so \(2^k\mid\varphi(1)\) forces \(k=0\), and the second alternative holds with \(S\) empty.

## 2. The sharp lower bound at a power-of-two index

We now specialize the structural lemma to \(k=2^n\).

**Key lemma.** If \(m>0\) and
\[
2^{2^n}\mid\varphi(m),
\tag{10}
\]
then either
\[
m=F_n\quad\text{and }F_n\text{ is prime},
\tag{11}
\]
or
\[
m\ge2^{2^n+1}.
\tag{12}
\]

To prove this, apply the structural lemma with \(k=2^n\). If its first alternative holds, it immediately gives (12). Suppose instead that
\[
m=\prod_{j\in S}F_j,
\tag{13}
\]
every \(F_j\) in the product is prime, and
\[
2^n\le\sum_{j\in S}2^j.
\tag{14}
\]

Not all indices in \(S\) can be strictly less than \(n\). Indeed, because \(S\) has no repeated indices, if every \(j\in S\) satisfied \(j<n\), then
\[
\sum_{j\in S}2^j
\le 1+2+\cdots+2^{n-1}
=2^n-1,
\]
contradicting (14). Therefore some \(j\in S\) satisfies \(j\ge n\).

First suppose that such a \(j\) is strictly larger than \(n\). Since \(j\ge n+1\),
\[
2^j\ge 2^{n+1}=2\cdot2^n\ge2^n+1.

after noting that \(2^n\ge1\). Therefore
\[
F_j=2^{2^j}+1\ge2^{2^j}\ge2^{2^n+1}.
\]
The factor \(F_j\) divides the positive integer \(m\), so \(m\ge F_j\), and (12) follows.

It remains to consider the case where the index found above is \(j=n\). If \(S=\{n\}\), then (13) gives \(m=F_n\), and the structural lemma also says that this Fermat number is prime. This is (11).

If \(S\) contains another index as well as \(n\), write
\[
m=F_nR,
\qquad
R=\prod_{i\in S\setminus\{n\}}F_i.
\]
The product defining \(R\) is nonempty. Every Fermat number is at least \(3\), so \(R\ge3\). Put \(x=2^{2^n}\). Then \(F_n=x+1\), and hence
\[
m=(x+1)R\ge3(x+1)\ge2x=2^{2^n+1}.
\]
Thus (12) again holds. This completes the proof of the key lemma.

## 3. Identification of the minimum

We now prove formula (1). There are two cases.

### Case 1: \(F_n\) is prime

Since \(F_n=2^{2^n}+1\), primality gives
\[
\varphi(F_n)=F_n-1=2^{2^n}.
\]
Thus \(F_n\) is an admissible member of the set defining \(A(2^n)\).

Let \(m>0\) be any other admissible integer, so that \(2^{2^n}\mid\varphi(m)\). By the key lemma, either \(m=F_n\), or
\[
m\ge2^{2^n+1}.
\]
But
\[
F_n=2^{2^n}+1\le2\cdot2^{2^n}=2^{2^n+1},
\]
since \(2^{2^n}\ge1\). Hence every admissible \(m\) is at least \(F_n\). Since \(F_n\) itself is admissible, it is the minimum:
\[
A(2^n)=F_n.
\]

### Case 2: \(F_n\) is not prime

Set
\[
M=2^{2^n+1}.
\]
Using \(\varphi(2^r)=2^{r-1}\) for \(r\ge1\), we obtain
\[
\varphi(M)=\varphi\bigl(2^{2^n+1}\bigr)=2^{2^n}.
\]
Therefore \(M\) is admissible for the minimum defining \(A(2^n)\).

Now let \(m>0\) be any admissible integer. The key lemma says that either \(m=F_n\) with \(F_n\) prime, or \(m\ge2^{2^n+1}\). The first possibility is excluded by the present assumption that \(F_n\) is not prime. Consequently every admissible \(m\) satisfies \(m\ge M\). Since \(M\) itself is admissible,
\[
A(2^n)=2^{2^n+1}.
\]

This proves (1) for every \(n\).

Finally, put \(n=33\). Then the index in the sequence is
\[
2^{33}=8589934592,
\]
and
\[
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
A(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&\text{if }F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is the conjectured value.
